# A sharp dimension drop for covers through an exterior or boundary contact

Let `d>=2`, let K be a d-dimensional convex body, and let
`y notin int(K)`. Suppose finitely many closed halfspaces `H_1,...,H_N`
have their boundaries through y and cover all of `R^d`. Then
\[
 \boxed{\quad \max_i |K\cap H_i|\ge\gamma_{d-1}|K|,
 \qquad \gamma_{d-1}=\left(\frac{d-1}{d}\right)^{d-1}.\quad}
\tag{1}
\]
The constant is sharp both when y lies strictly outside K and when y is
on its boundary. The proof uses the exact projective density; it does
not replace it by uniform measure on the projected support.

## 1. A radial-integral convexity lemma at the required negative power

Let `p>=1` and let f be a bounded, nonnegative, upper-semicontinuous
function of compact support in a Euclidean space. Assume its positive
set has nonempty interior and
\[
 f^{-1/(p+1)}
\]
is convex as an extended-real function, with value infinity where f is
zero. Set, for nonzero x,
\[
 I_p(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}f(tx)\,dt.
\]
Then
\[
 U_p=\{0\}\cup\{x\ne0:I_p(x)\ge1\}
\tag{2}
\]
is a compact convex set. At nonzero x its gauge is `I_p(x)^(-1/p)`,
interpreted as infinity when the integral is zero; its gauge at zero is
defined to be zero. If f is positive in a neighborhood
of zero, U_p is a convex body containing zero in its interior.

Crucially, positivity at zero is **not needed for convexity** in (2).
The ray's positive interval is permitted to start at a positive radius.

Here is the full inequality proof. Take x_1,x_2 with `I_p(x_i)=1` and
`0<lambda<1`. The positive radial intervals of f on these rays are
intervals, because its positive set is convex. Its restriction is
positive and continuous in each such interval's relative interior:
this follows by restricting the finite convex function
`f^(-1/(p+1))` to that line. Thus the probability densities
\[
 R^{p-1}f(Rx_1)\,dR,\qquad S^{p-1}f(Sx_2)\,dS
\]
have continuously differentiable increasing quantiles R(v),S(v),
`0<v<1`. Put
\[
 T=\left(\frac\lambda R+\frac{1-\lambda}S\right)^{-1},
 \quad a=\frac{\lambda T}{R},\quad b=\frac{(1-\lambda)T}{S}.
\]
Then `a,b>0`, `a+b=1`, `T=aR+bS`, and for
`x=lambda x_1+(1-lambda)x_2`,
\[
 Tx=aRx_1+bSx_2.
\]
If x=0, the conclusion is immediate from its inclusion in (2). Otherwise
convexity of the negative power gives, writing `f_1=f(Rx_1)`,
`f_2=f(Sx_2)`,
\[
 f(Tx)\ge
 \left(a f_1^{-1/(p+1)}+b f_2^{-1/(p+1)}\right)^{-(p+1)}.
\tag{3}
\]
Differentiating the quantiles and T gives
\[
 R'=\frac1{R^{p-1}f_1},\quad
 S'=\frac1{S^{p-1}f_2},\quad
 T'=T^2\left(\frac{\lambda R'}{R^2}
             +\frac{(1-\lambda)S'}{S^2}\right)>0.
\]
Hölder's inequality, applied with weights a,b and exponents p+1 and
`(p+1)/p`, states exactly
\[
 \left(a f_1^{-1/(p+1)}+b f_2^{-1/(p+1)}\right)^{p+1}
 \le\left(\frac a{R^pf_1}+\frac b{S^pf_2}\right)(aR+bS)^p.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed write each term `f_i^(-1/(p+1))` as
`(R_i^(-p)f_i^(-1))^(1/(p+1)) R_i^(p/(p+1))`.
Equations (3)–(4) give
\[
 T^{p-1}f(Tx)T'
 =T^pf(Tx)\left(\frac a{R^pf_1}+\frac b{S^pf_2}\right)\ge1.
\]
Integrating over `0<v<1` and changing variable by the strictly increasing
T proves `I_p(x)>=1`. When the original rays begin away from zero,
the change of variables merely integrates over an interval with a
positive lower endpoint; that integral is still bounded above by the
full integral defining I_p. Thus no origin-in-support assumption has
entered.

Positive homogeneity `I_p(cx)=c^(-p)I_p(x)` extends the boundary-segment
argument to all points of U_p: write points as contractions of their
radial boundary points, combine them, and contract once more toward zero.
This proves convexity. Compact support and boundedness of f give a
uniform upper bound for I_p on the unit sphere, hence boundedness of U_p.
For a converging sequence of nonzero directions, the support bound restricts
all radial integrals to one finite interval; upper semicontinuity of f
and the dominated upper-limit inequality therefore give upper
semicontinuity of I_p. This includes a ray that misses the positive
support: its integral is zero, its gauge is infinite, and nearby radial
extents tend to zero. A ray contained in a support face may instead
have a positive radial interval; that interval is retained. These facts
prove U_p is closed and treat its boundary radial limits. If f
is positive near zero, an inner ball and a positive lower density on a
smaller ball give a uniform positive radial lower bound, completing the
last assertion.

## 2. A sharp centerpoint theorem for the projective density class

Let `r>=1`. Suppose f is as in Section 1, is positive in the interior of
its full-dimensional convex support, and
\[
 f^{-1/(r+1)}\text{ is convex}.
\]
Then f has a point whose every containing closed halfspace has f-mass
at least `gamma_r integral f`.

We prove this statement rather than presume that such a density is
log-concave. Normalize `integral f=1`. Its depth at a point is the
minimum, over unit u, of
\[
 P(u,y)=\int_{u\cdot(x-y)\ge0}f(x)\,dx.
\]
It suffices to consider boundaries through y, since moving any containing
halfspace to y can only reduce its mass. The function P is jointly
continuous in u,y by dominated convergence: every limiting hyperplane
has Lebesgue measure zero. Compactness of the unit sphere therefore
makes its minimum continuous. The depth vanishes on and outside the
boundary of the closed convex support, by an outward supporting
halfspace. It is strictly positive at every interior point, because f
has a positive lower bound on a small ball around that point. Hence a
maximum alpha is attained at an interior point y_*.

The active unit normals
\[
 A=\{u:P(u,y_*)=\alpha\}
\]
form a nonempty compact set. They have zero in their convex hull.
Here are the full uniform details. Otherwise strict separation gives a
v and delta>0 with `u.v>=delta` on A. Let
`O={u:u.v>delta/2}`. On the compact complement of O, the cap mass at y_*
exceeds alpha by one fixed eta>0. Choose a ball `B(y_*,R)` on which
`f>=m>0`; such constants exist because the finite positive convex
function `f^(-1/(r+1))` is continuous near the interior point y_*.
For `epsilon|v|<=R/2` and every u in O, moving the anchor to
`y_*-epsilon v` adds a slab of thickness at least `epsilon delta/2`.
Its sections within this ball have (r-1)-volume at least
`omega_(r-1)(R/2)^(r-1)`, with `omega_0=1`. Thus every such cap gains
at least `m epsilon delta omega_(r-1)(R/2)^(r-1)/2>0`, uniformly.
For sufficiently small epsilon, joint continuity uniformly keeps all
caps outside O above `alpha+eta/2`. The minimum over all normals has
therefore increased, a contradiction. Finite-dimensional Carathéodory
supplies active normals
`u_1,...,u_m`, `m<=r+1`, and positive weights summing to one with
\[
 \sum_i\lambda_i u_i=0.
\tag{5}
\]

Translate y_* to zero and apply Section 1 with `p=r` to this translated
f. Translation preserves convexity of its negative power. The resulting
convex radial body can be scaled to have radial function
\[
 \rho(\omega)^r=r\int_0^\infty f(t\omega)t^{r-1}\,dt.
\]
Polar integration gives its volume one and, for **every** halfspace
through zero, the same mass as f. In particular the active caps from
(5) each cut volume alpha from this convex body U. They cover all of
`R^r`, because for every point at least one of the scalar products
`u_i.x` is nonnegative. Hence every point w of U belongs to one of these
mass-alpha closed caps, and its depth in U is at most alpha. At zero,
all through-point cap fractions agree with those of f at y_*, so its
depth equals alpha. Thus zero is itself a deepest point of U; it has
not been asserted to be U's centroid. Applying the classical continuous
Grünbaum inequality at the actual centroid of U gives a point of depth
at least gamma_r. Consequently `alpha>=gamma_r`. This proves the
claimed centerpoint theorem for the entire stated negative-power
density class.

All uses of radial and polar integration are of bounded measurable
functions on bounded sets. Halfspace boundaries carry zero mass.

## 3. Strictly exterior contacts and their exact central projection

Translate the given contact y to zero and suppose first that `0 notin K`.
Strict separation allows orthonormal coordinates `(t,x) in R x R^(d-1)`
and constants `0<a<=b<infinity` such that every point of K has
`a<=t<=b`. One direct construction takes the direction from zero to its
closest point of K; its scalar product with every point of K is strictly
positive.

The map `(t,s)->(t,ts)` for `t>0` has Jacobian `t^(d-1)`. Thus the
central projection of uniform volume on K to `t=1` has the **exact**
density
\[
 \phi(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{d-1}1_K(t,ts)\,dt,
 \qquad \int\phi=|K|.
\tag{6}
\]
It is bounded, has compact convex support, is positive on the support's
interior, and is upper semicontinuous. Boundedness and compactness follow
from `a<=t<=b`; upper semicontinuity follows from that of the indicator
of the closed body K and the dominated upper-limit inequality. Positivity
on the projection interior follows by projecting the interior of K;
for a full-dimensional convex body this image is exactly the interior
of its projection. To see the latter fact directly, fix an interior
point `(t_0,t_0s_0)` of K. An interior projected point s can be written
as `lambda s_0+(1-lambda)s_1`, with `0<lambda<1` and s_1 in the
projection. Choose `(t_1,t_1s_1)` in K and combine these original points
with weights proportional to `lambda/t_0` and `(1-lambda)/t_1`. The
result lies in int K and projects to s. The ray therefore has a
positive interval inside K, proving phi(s)>0.

To identify the relevant concavity, apply Section 1 with `p=d` and
`f=1_K` in dimension d. Its negative power is the convex extended-real
function equal to one on K and infinity outside K. The resulting
radial gauge is convex, including when zero is outside K. Restrict that
gauge to the affine plane `(1,s)` to obtain
\[
 \boxed{\quad \phi(s)^{-1/d}\text{ is convex}.\quad}
\tag{7}
\]
The exponent is exactly `-1/(r+1)` for `r=d-1`, not an assertion of
ordinary log-concavity of the projected density.

Every original halfspace through zero restricts on `t=1` to a closed
affine halfspace in `R^(d-1)`, or to all or none of that space. The
restricted family covers that whole space, since the original family
covers `R^d`. If one restriction is all space, its original cap contains
all of K and (1) is immediate. Otherwise ignore the empty restrictions
and apply Section 2 to phi. Its guaranteed center belongs to at least
one of the remaining projected halfspaces, which therefore has phi-mass
at least `gamma_(d-1)|K|`. Since `t>0`, membership in each homogeneous
original halfspace is exactly membership of s in its restricted
halfspace. Equation (6) transfers that mass back to the original cap
and proves (1) for a strictly exterior contact.

## 4. Contacts on the boundary

Suppose now y lies on `partial K`. Choose a supporting unit normal e
with `e.(x-y)>=0` on K, and put `y_epsilon=y-epsilon e`. This point
lies strictly outside K. Write the original halfspaces as
\[
 H_i=\{x:a_i\cdot(x-y)\ge0\},\qquad a_i\ne0.
\]
For every positive epsilon their simultaneous translations
\[
 H_{i,\epsilon}=\{x:a_i\cdot(x-y_\epsilon)\ge0\}
\]
still cover `R^d` and share the exterior contact y_epsilon. Section 3
therefore gives an index with cap volume at least `gamma_(d-1)|K|`.
Along a sequence epsilon tending to zero, one fixed index occurs
infinitely often. Its halfspaces converge to the original H_i, and the
indicators converge almost everywhere on K because the limiting
hyperplane has d-volume zero. Dominated convergence proves the same
inequality for H_i. This treats all boundary contacts without discarding
any positive volume and without requiring a finite projected density
at a boundary anchor.

## 5. Sharpness for exterior and boundary contacts

Put `r=d-1`, and let T be an r-simplex in `R^r` with centroid zero.
Let `beta_0,...,beta_r` be the gradients of its barycentric coordinates.
Then `sum beta_i=0`, and each simplex centroid cap
`{s:beta_i.s>=0}` has volume fraction
\[
 \left(\frac r{r+1}\right)^r=\gamma_r.
\]
This is the simplex homothety computation: the cap is the copy of T
scaled by `r/(r+1)` about the corresponding vertex.

For a strictly exterior example take the cone frustum
\[
 K=\{(t,x):1\le t\le2,\quad x\in tT\},\qquad y=0.
\]
This is a full-dimensional compact convex body and y is outside it.
Use the d closed halfspaces `H_i={beta_i.x>=0}`. Their normals are
nonzero, their boundaries pass through y, and their union is all of
`R^d`, because their weighted scalar products sum to zero. On every
positive t-slice their cap fraction is exactly gamma_r, so every H_i
has that exact fraction of the full volume of K. This proves sharpness
of (1) with a strictly exterior nominated contact. The normals in this
exact equality example have rank d-1; their common boundary intersection
is the t-axis, which also meets K. The theorem permits that situation.
No full-rank or unique-common-contact equality statement is being made.

For a boundary example replace the interval `[1,2]` by `[0,1]`. The
result is a pyramid with apex y=0, and the same calculation and same
full-space cover give equality. In particular the sharp constants are
one half in dimension two and four ninths in dimension three.

In dimension one the analogous statement has constant gamma_0=1 and
follows directly: an interval lying entirely on one side of an exterior
or endpoint contact is contained in the halfline of that orientation,
and a full-line cover by halfspaces through the contact includes that
orientation. No zero-dimensional radial formula is needed.

## 6. Full-rank unique-contact examples approaching the same constant

The same optimal constant cannot be improved by requiring a unique
common contact and full-rank normals, although the preceding exact
equality family did not have those properties. In either sharpness body,
replace the normal `(0,beta_0)` by the two normals
\[
 (\epsilon,\beta_0),\qquad(-\epsilon,\beta_0),
\]
and retain `(0,beta_i)` for `1<=i<=r`. Give the new pair weights one
and the remaining normals weights two. Their sum is zero, so their
closed halfspaces still cover all of `R^d`. Their span is full d:
the difference of the new pair gives the t-axis normal, and the
continuous barycentric gradients span `R^r`. Their common boundary
intersection is therefore exactly the nominated point zero.

For `0<epsilon<min(1/(r+1),r/(r+1))`, the projected cuts of the new pair
are `beta_0.s>=-epsilon` and `beta_0.s>=epsilon`. Since
`lambda_0(s)=1/(r+1)+beta_0.s`, their exact volume fractions are
\[
 \left(\frac r{r+1}+\epsilon\right)^r,
 \qquad
 \left(\frac r{r+1}-\epsilon\right)^r.
\]
Every other fraction is gamma_r. Consequently the maximum fraction
tends to gamma_r from above as epsilon decreases to zero. This proves
sharpness as an infimum within the full-rank, unique-contact subclass,
for both strictly exterior and boundary contacts. It makes no claim
of equality at a positive epsilon.

## 7. A precise positive-circuit consequence for one mixed fiber

Let a positive d-dimensional fiber K_z have volume w_z. Suppose a
subfamily of ambient caps has one actual common continuous contact y
on that fiber plane, and its continuous normals admit strictly positive
weights with zero weighted sum. Thus their restricted margins are
`u_i.(x-y)` and their positive weighted sum is identically zero.
They cover the whole continuous space. If `y notin int K_z`, (1) gives
\[
 \max_i\mu(H_i)\ge\max_i|K_z\cap H_i|
 \ge\gamma_{d-1}w_z.
\]
Consequently, if every cap in that circuit has total mixed mass strictly
below `gamma_(d-1) w_z`, its common contact must lie in the interior of
K_z. The conclusion retains the actual circuit and its positive weights;
it does not manufacture one common point from differently supported
contact measures or assert that a sufficiently heavy fiber exists.
